name: hashcash
desc: Proof-of-work algorithm to counter denial-of-service (DoS) attacks
why: Proof-of-work stamps from the 1997 anti-spam scheme; a clear door into the idea behind Bitcoin mining and cost-based DoS defence.

brief.what_it_is: Hashcash is a proof-of-work algorithm and stamp format. A sender computes a stamp that takes a tunable amount of CPU work, and anyone can verify it cheaply. The input is a text to be stamped, such as an email, and the output is a stamp that proves the work was done. The homepage says the algorithm works with a cryptographic hash such as SHA1 or SHA256, and that a stamp can be checked by counting leading zeros with ordinary tools like sha1sum. The same name also covers an email anti-spam tool that attaches stamps to mail, and a library form of the code.
brief.why_it_exists: It is a denial-of-service counter-measure: it adds a small, unavoidable cost to actions that are cheap to spam, such as sending mail. The homepage frames it as 'payment in burnt CPU cycles' that can throttle abuse of un-metered resources while preserving privacy, and as a stop-gap until electronic cash is widely used.
brief.how_it_works: The sender searches for a value that makes a hash of the stamped data have a set number of leading zero bits, which is a partial hash collision. Each extra bit doubles the average work, and verification is a single hash. The cypherspace page gives the example of a 20-bit collision taking about 6 seconds on a machine testing 180,000 hashes per second. The homepage notes that the work needed should rise a couple of bits a year as machines get faster.
brief.install_notes: Neither page gives installation steps or commands. The cypherspace page, which is the older location, lists prebuilt tool binaries for Windows win32 and redhat9-i386 (rpm and tgz formats), a .src.rpm buildable on any Unix RPM platform, and source with a Visual C++ project file. It also lists a Windows GUI build, and third-party versions in Java, a browser applet, RISC-OS, Emacs (hashcash.el), and Perl. The homepage says the site is moving to hashcash.org, so some links may be stale. The brew metadata lists two executables, hashcash and sha1, but neither page mentions sha1.
brief.standout: The verification step is so simple that a human can check a stamp by counting leading zeros with sha1sum, and the whole scheme can be re-implemented from scratch in a few lines. Its design, from 1997, is the ancestor of the proof-of-work idea that Bitcoin mining later used, and the homepage says that is now its most widely used role.
brief.status: Unknown, leaning quiet. The homepage has a 'hits since nov 03' counter and the cypherspace page has a 'new 1-Sep-2003' counter, and the paper is dated Aug 2002. The pages show no release version or recent commit dates, and I did not check a source repository. The site is described as being 'slowly moving' to a new domain.
brief.caveats: Most of the material is old, dating from about 2002 to 2003, and the binaries listed are for Windows and RedHat 9. The homepage says Microsoft released an incompatible hashcash spec (email postmark) that hashes the body too, uses a modified SHA1, and uses multiple sub-puzzles. The homepage also warns that hashcash 'suffers from a high rate of inflation' as machines get faster, so the difficulty must keep rising. The sha1 executable from the brew metadata is not documented on either page.
quotes: A hashcash stamp constitutes a proof-of-work which takes a parameterizable amount of work to compute for the sender.
Hash cash is payment in burnt CPU cycles by calculating n-bit partial hash collisions on chosen texts.
Verification can be done by a human eye (count leading 0s) even with availability of common preinstalled command line tools such as sha1sum.
